title: Where old maps put the Great Lakes
hook: Eleven maps from 1688 to 1818 placed the same 39 lakeshore points. Which way did they miss?

doesNotKnow: that the error was mostly east-west
that it shrank within a century

misconception: Old maps were equally wrong in every direction.
objective: The learner can say that old maps of the Great Lakes were wrong mostly east-west (Coronelli 1688: about 6 times the north-south error) and that the east-west error shrank by 1818, because longitude needs a time difference while latitude does not.

claims.text: The latitude and longitude of 39 Great Lakes points as read from 11 maps (Coronelli 1688 to Melish 1818), and their actual positions.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: oldmaps, OldMaps.csv, columns lat and long (Andrews & Herzberg 1985, Table 10.1, per the HistData doc). Absolute values used because of sign typos noted in the doc; copied into Demo.tsx as ACTUAL and MAPS.

claims.text: On Coronelli's 1688 map the points were on average 59 km off north-south but 363 km off east-west; on Melish's 1818 map the east-west error was 41 km (north-south 24 km); east-west was the worse error on 9 of the 11 maps.
claims.source: history-cycle1-check.mjs section 10: north-south = |dlat| x 111.32 km, east-west = |dlon| x 111.32 x cos(actual latitude), mean over 39 points. Coronelli 59 / 363 (x6.2), Melish 24 / 41, 9 of 11 (not Mitchell 1755 or Lattre 1784). Demo.tsx computes the same; stage and reveal both round to whole km (the brief's draft reveal rounded to tens: 60, 360, 40).

claims.text: Latitude can be taken from the height of the Sun or a star, while longitude needs a time difference.
claims.source: Brief #10 claim (3): the longitude problem (prerequisite geography:sun-time-from-longitude; 15 degrees of longitude per hour of Earth's rotation). Not opened against a primary source by the builder.

claims.text: Where it stops: each map's 39 points were read off by hand.
claims.source: history-data.mjs: oldmaps, HistData OldMaps documentation (opened per the brief): points read from the maps with a grid overlay and linear interpolation.

claims.text: The map is drawn on a conic equal-area projection over the Great Lakes (parallels 42 and 47 N), with today's country outlines from Natural Earth 1:110m.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: geoConicEqualArea().parallels([42, 47]).rotate([84, 0]) from d3-geo via @/kit/geo; outlines from the kit's world-atlas 110m countries (coarse; lakes are not cut out). Outlines are context only; every error is computed from the point coordinates, not from the drawing.

recall.question: A sailor in 1700 knows her latitude exactly but her clock is 20 minutes wrong. Which way is her position uncertain?
recall.why: A clock error is a longitude error: 20 minutes of time is 5 degrees of longitude, east or west.
